2. SimpleGraph🔗

In this chapter we introduce the basics of SimpleGraph, Mathlib's definition of a simple, loopless, undirected graph. We will explore how adjacency, edges, darts, and neighbourhoods are defined. We will also look at the process of constructing a graph (the infinite path on ℕ) using a few different methods. Finally we will look at how to perform basic computations on graphs.

2.1. SimpleGraph🔗

Mathlib already contains a few different definitions of graphs (for example directed graphs as Digraph and multigraphs as Graph), but we will only look at SimpleGraph. Although SimpleGraph is currently the most commonly used graph structure in Mathlib, it has some real limitations: for example any non-spanning subgraph of a SimpleGraph V is not a SimpleGraph V. However, it has a well-developed API and many results can be formalized with relative ease.

The definition of SimpleGraph in Mathlib says that, for a fixed vertex type V, a term of SimpleGraph V is a structure consisting of a binary relation Adj on V that tells us which pairs of vertices are adjacent, and two proofs symm and loopless that this relation is symmetric and irreflexive. We can omit proofs of symm and loopless and Lean will try to fill them in using the automated aesop_graph tactic. Note that V is a parameter of the structure rather than one of its fields: graphs on different vertex types have different types.

section basics variable {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) @[ext, aesop safe constructors (rule_sets := [SimpleGraph]), wikidata Q141488] structure SimpleGraph (V : Type u) where /-- The adjacency relation of a simple graph. -/ Adj : V → V → Prop symm : Std.Symm Adj := by aesop_graph loopless : Std.Irrefl Adj := by aesop_graph#source SimpleGraph -- structure SimpleGraph (V : Type u) where -- Adj : V → V → Prop -- symm : Std.Symm Adj := by aesop_graph -- loopless : Std.Irrefl Adj := by aesop_graph G.Adj : V → V → Prop#check G.Adj -- a relation on V describing adjacency in G G.symm : Std.Symm G.Adj#check G.symm -- adjacency is symmetric (undirected edges) G.loopless : Std.Irrefl G.Adj#check G.loopless -- adjacency is irreflexive (no loops)

Both Std.Symm Adj and Std.Irrefl Adj are structures with a single field, namely symm : ∀ a b, Adj a b → Adj b a and irrefl : ∀ a, ¬Adj a a. So to give these proofs by hand we write symm := ⟨fun a b h => …⟩ (or give a tactic proof with symm := by constructor; …).

We will meet the formal definition of a graph's edges in a moment, but usually we reason directly with the adjacency relation G.Adj. Informally we write u — v for an edge of G joining u and v; in Lean we instead work with a proof h of the proposition G.Adj u v : Prop. (Strictly speaking, h : G.Adj u v records the directed edge u → v, but by symmetry it also gives G.Adj v u, namely h.symm, so we can treat it as the undirected edge u — v.)

example {u v : V} (h : G.Adj u v) : G.Adj v u := h.symm

The fact that G does not have a loop at a vertex u is the proposition ¬ G.Adj u u.

example {u : V} : ¬ G.Adj u u := G.irrefl

2.2. Edges🔗

Since SimpleGraph is a loopless undirected graph, its edges are unordered pairs of distinct vertices. In Lean unordered pairs have type Sym2 V, the symmetric square of V. Formally this is the quotient of V × V modulo swaps (Sym2.Rel). Elements (or more precisely terms) of Sym2 V are denoted s(u, v). Note that although s(v, v) cannot be an edge of a SimpleGraph (which is loopless), the type Sym2 V still contains such pairs.

example {u v : V} : s(u, v) = s(v, u) := Sym2.eq_swap

The edge set of G is G.edgeSet and is a Set (Sym2 V). Membership is definitionally equivalent to adjacency. (This means that the proof is rfl.)

example {u v : V} : s(u, v) ∈ G.edgeSet ↔ G.Adj u v := V:Type u_1G:SimpleGraph Vu:Vv:V⊢ s(u, v) ∈ G.edgeSet ↔ G.Adj u v All goals completed! 🐙

However using G.Adj u v has a couple of advantages over s(u, v) ∈ G.edgeSet: it avoids the need for Sym2 V and, via dot notation, we have easy access to convenient lemmas about adjacency.

SimpleGraph.Adj.ne.{u} {V : Type u} {G : SimpleGraph V} {a b : V} (h : G.Adj a b) : a ≠ b#check Adj.ne -- G.Adj a b → a ≠ b example {u v : V} (h : G.Adj u v) : u ≠ v := h.ne example {u v : V} (h : G.Adj u v) : v ≠ u := h.ne'

Generally we prefer to use G.Adj u v rather than s(u, v) ∈ G.edgeSet when talking about individual edges, but when we want to talk about a set of (possible) edges of a graph then s : Set (Sym2 V) is what we need.

When we do need to prove something about an arbitrary e : Sym2 V, the usual first step is induction e using Sym2.ind. Every term of Sym2 V is s(x, y) for some x y : V, and Sym2.ind reduces the goal to that case. For example, no edge of G is a loop. Mathlib calls a pair of the form s(v, v) diagonal (Sym2.IsDiag).

example (e : Sym2 V) (he : e ∈ G.edgeSet) : ¬ e.IsDiag := V:Type u_1G:SimpleGraph Ve:Sym2 Vhe:e ∈ G.edgeSet⊢ ¬e.IsDiag induction e using Sym2.ind with V:Type u_1G:SimpleGraph Vx:Vy:Vhe:s(x, y) ∈ G.edgeSet⊢ ¬s(x, y).IsDiag -- he : s(x, y) ∈ G.edgeSet ⊢ ¬s(x, y).IsDiag V:Type u_1G:SimpleGraph Vx:Vy:Vhe:G.Adj x y⊢ ¬s(x, y).IsDiag V:Type u_1G:SimpleGraph Vx:Vy:Vhe:G.Adj x y⊢ ¬x = y All goals completed! 🐙

Notice that induction replaced e by s(x, y) in the hypothesis he as well as in the goal. This result is G.not_isDiag_of_mem_edgeSet in Mathlib.

2.3. Vertices🔗

The vertex set of a SimpleGraph V is V (although strictly speaking V is a type, not a set). These can be infinite (ℕ), or empty (Fin 0). Nonemptiness and finiteness are extra hypotheses that need to be stated: for example as [Nonempty V] and [Fintype V]. See Decidability, Finiteness and Degrees for more details.

Mathlib defines a number of useful subsets of V (terms s : Set V), in particular the support of the graph and the neighborSet of a vertex. (We can refer to the entire vertex set of a SimpleGraph V as a set by Set.univ : Set V.)

2.3.1. Support🔗

The support of a graph is the set of vertices that belong to at least one edge.

SimpleGraph.mem_support.{u} {V : Type u} (G : SimpleGraph V) {v : V} : v ∈ G.support ↔ ∃ w, G.Adj v w#check mem_support -- (G : SimpleGraph V) {v : V} : v ∈ G.support ↔ ∃ w, G.Adj v w

If G.Adj u v then u is in the support of G.

example {u v : V} (h : G.Adj u v) : u ∈ G.support := h.left_mem_support

Notice that in the previous example we could use h.left_mem_support where h : G.Adj u v since the theorem we applied is in the SimpleGraph.Adj namespace. Also note the use of "left" in the name of the lemma. You should be able to guess how to prove v ∈ G.support from h : G.Adj u v.

SimpleGraph.Adj.left_mem_support.{u} {V : Type u} (G : SimpleGraph V) {u v : V} (hadj : G.Adj u v) : u ∈ G.support#check SimpleGraph.Adj.left_mem_support

2.3.2. Neighbours🔗

The neighbours of a vertex v in a graph G are the vertices adjacent to v.

def neighborSet (v : V) : Set V := {w | G.Adj v w}#source neighborSet -- def neighborSet (v : V) : Set V := {w | G.Adj v w} example {u v : V} : G.Adj u v ↔ v ∈ G.neighborSet u := V:Type u_1G:SimpleGraph Vu:Vv:V⊢ G.Adj u v ↔ v ∈ G.neighborSet u All goals completed! 🐙 example {u : V} : G.neighborSet u ⊆ G.support := V:Type u_1G:SimpleGraph Vu:V⊢ G.neighborSet u ⊆ G.support V:Type u_1G:SimpleGraph Vu:Vv:Vhv:v ∈ G.neighborSet u⊢ v ∈ G.support All goals completed! 🐙

This result is also in Mathlib.

example {u : V} : G.neighborSet u ⊆ G.support := G.neighborSet_subset_support u

The incidence set of v is the set of edges that contain v. (For e : Sym2 V, v ∈ e means that v is one of the two endpoints of e.) A vertex is isolated if it has no neighbours; it is universal if it is adjacent to every other vertex.

def incidenceSet (v : V) : Set (Sym2 V) := { e ∈ G.edgeSet | v ∈ e }#source incidenceSet -- {e ∈ G.edgeSet | v ∈ e} SimpleGraph.mem_incidenceSet.{u} {V : Type u} (G : SimpleGraph V) (v w : V) : s(v, w) ∈ G.incidenceSet v ↔ G.Adj v w#check mem_incidenceSet -- s(v, w) ∈ G.incidenceSet v ↔ G.Adj v w def IsIsolated (G : SimpleGraph V) (v : V) : Prop := ∀ w, ¬ G.Adj v w#source IsIsolated -- ∀ w, ¬G.Adj v w def IsUniversal (G : SimpleGraph V) (v : V) : Prop := ∀ ⦃w⦄, v ≠ w → G.Adj v w#source IsUniversal -- ∀ ⦃w⦄, v ≠ w → G.Adj v w

The braces ∀ ⦃w⦄ in the definition of IsUniversal mark w as a strict-implicit argument: Lean fills it in like {w}, but only once a later explicit argument (here the proof of v ≠ w) is supplied.

2.3.2.1. Sets as Types🔗

Although G.neighborSet u is a Set V, Lean also lets us use it as a type. A term w : G.neighborSet u is a vertex together with a proof that this vertex is a neighbour of u.

Lean displays this type as ↑(G.neighborSet u): it is the subtype {w : V // w ∈ G.neighborSet u}. We build such terms with the anonymous constructor ⟨v, h⟩ and take them apart with .val (the vertex) and .property (the proof). Lean inserts .val automatically wherever a term of V is expected, and displays it as ↑w.

example {u v : V} (h : G.Adj u v) : G.neighborSet u := ⟨v, h⟩ example {u : V} (w : G.neighborSet u) : G.Adj u w.val := V:Type u_1G:SimpleGraph Vu:Vw:↑(G.neighborSet u)⊢ G.Adj u ↑w All goals completed! 🐙 example {u : V} (w : G.neighborSet u) : G.Adj u w := V:Type u_1G:SimpleGraph Vu:Vw:↑(G.neighborSet u)⊢ G.Adj u ↑w All goals completed! 🐙

2.4. Darts🔗

Since edges in SimpleGraph are undirected it might seem strange to introduce the notion of a dart (an oriented edge). However we already noted that h : G.Adj u v has a direction to it; darts simply give us a way to talk about the ordered pairs of adjacent vertices in a graph. These can be very useful, for example in double counting arguments such as proving the handshake lemma.

A dart d : G.Dart is an ordered pair of vertices together with a proof that they are adjacent in G. Since edges are unoriented, darts come in symmetric pairs: if d : G.Dart then d.symm is the opposite dart and d.edge is the edge corresponding to d.

section darts structure Dart extends V × V where adj : G.Adj fst snd deriving DecidableEq#source Dart variable (d : G.Dart) d.toProd.1 : V#check d.fst -- the first vertex of the dart d.toProd.2 : V#check d.snd -- the second vertex of the dart d.adj : G.Adj d.toProd.1 d.toProd.2#check d.adj -- the adjacency proof of the dart d.edge : Sym2 V#check d.edge -- the edge corresponding to the dart d.symm : G.Dart#check d.symm -- the opposite dart from d.snd to d.fst

Edges are unoriented so d and d.symm correspond to the same edge.

example : d.symm.edge = d.edge := Dart.edge_symm d example : d.fst = d.symm.snd := rfl end darts

2.5. Naming Conventions🔗

We have now met a few Mathlib names, and they follow fixed patterns. Knowing the rules will help us guess a lemma's name. The full rules can be found in Mathlib's naming conventions. The key points are:

  • Theorems are named in snake_case, predicates and structures in UpperCamelCase (IsIsolated, Dart) and other definitions in lowerCamelCase (neighborSet).

  • A theorem's name describes its statement, with the conclusion first and any hypotheses after of. Symbols have standard names: ¬ is not, ∈ is mem, ⊆ is subset, ≠ is ne, ∉ is notMem and ⊤ is top. So not_isDiag_of_mem_edgeSet says that an edge e ∈ G.edgeSet is not a loop, and neighborSet_subset_support says that G.neighborSet u ⊆ G.support.

  • An equivalence (↔) that characterises membership of a set, such as mem_edgeSet or mem_support, is named after its left-hand side alone. Other equivalences often end in _iff, such as Sym2.mk_isDiag_iff.

  • A theorem about h : G.Adj u v lives in the namespace SimpleGraph.Adj, so we can use it with dot notation, as with h.ne and h.left_mem_support. A prime marks a minor variant, so h.ne proves u ≠ v while h.ne' proves v ≠ u.

When the rules don't allow us to guess the name, we can search for it as described in Finding Lemmas.

2.6. Order🔗

There is a partial order on SimpleGraph V given by G ≤ H iff G is a subgraph of H. Note that these are necessarily spanning subgraphs since all SimpleGraph V have the same vertex set. We will consider general subgraphs later, see Subgraphs.

This gives SimpleGraph V the structure of a complete atomic Boolean algebra, with operations sup (⊔), inf (⊓), compl (ᶜ) and sdiff (\), and elements top (⊤) and bot (⊥). This terminology comes from order theory rather than graph theory, but it is very natural in the context of formalization. Here complete means that every set of graphs in SimpleGraph V has a supremum (the graph whose edges are those present in at least one graph in the set) and an infimum (the graph whose edges are those present in every graph in the set). The atoms of SimpleGraph V are the graphs with exactly one edge, and atomic means that every graph is the supremum of the atoms below it, i.e. the union of its single-edge subgraphs. Mathlib registers this structure as an instance, which Lean supplies automatically wherever it is needed. The command #synth asks Lean to find (synthesize) an instance and shows it; we will say more about instances in Decidability, Finiteness and Degrees.

section order completeAtomicBooleanAlgebra#synth CompleteAtomicBooleanAlgebra (SimpleGraph V) instance : LE (SimpleGraph V) where le x y := ∀ ⦃v w : V⦄, x.Adj v w → y.Adj v w#source SimpleGraph.instLE -- le x y := ∀ ⦃v w : V⦄, x.Adj v w → y.Adj v w variable (H : SimpleGraph V) G ≤ H : Prop#check G ≤ H

The definition of proper subgraph (G < H) is phrased differently to how we might expect. Rather than G < H ↔ G ≤ H ∧ G ≠ H we have:

example : G < H ↔ G ≤ H ∧ ¬ H ≤ G := V:Type u_1G:SimpleGraph VH:SimpleGraph V⊢ G < H ↔ G ≤ H ∧ ¬H ≤ G All goals completed! 🐙

Of course they are equivalent.

example : G < H ↔ G ≤ H ∧ G ≠ H := lt_iff_le_and_ne

The sup of G and H, denoted G ⊔ H, is the SimpleGraph V in which any pair of vertices from V are adjacent iff they are adjacent in G or H (i.e. it is the union of G and H).

SimpleGraph.sup_adj.{u} {V : Type u} (x y : SimpleGraph V) (v w : V) : (x ⊔ y).Adj v w ↔ x.Adj v w ∨ y.Adj v w#check sup_adj

The inf of G and H, denoted G ⊓ H, is the SimpleGraph V in which any pair of vertices from V are adjacent iff they are adjacent in both G and H (i.e. it is the intersection of G and H).

SimpleGraph.inf_adj.{u} {V : Type u} (x y : SimpleGraph V) (v w : V) : (x ⊓ y).Adj v w ↔ x.Adj v w ∧ y.Adj v w#check inf_adj

The complement of G, denoted Gᶜ, is the SimpleGraph V in which the edges are all pairs of distinct vertices that are not adjacent in G.

SimpleGraph.compl_adj.{u} {V : Type u} (G : SimpleGraph V) (v w : V) : Gᶜ.Adj v w ↔ v ≠ w ∧ ¬G.Adj v w#check compl_adj

The set difference of two graphs, denoted G \ H, has the edges of G with the edges of H removed. (Since the resulting graph is a SimpleGraph V the vertices are necessarily unchanged.)

SimpleGraph.sdiff_adj.{u} {V : Type u} (x y : SimpleGraph V) (v w : V) : (x \ y).Adj v w ↔ x.Adj v w ∧ ¬y.Adj v w#check sdiff_adj

We can remove a set of edges s : Set (Sym2 V) from a graph G to form G.deleteEdges s. If s = H.edgeSet then this is the same as the set difference G \ H.

def deleteEdges (s : Set (Sym2 V)) : SimpleGraph V := G \ fromEdgeSet s#source deleteEdges SimpleGraph.deleteEdges_adj.{u_1} {V : Type u_1} {v w : V} {G : SimpleGraph V} {s : Set (Sym2 V)} : (G.deleteEdges s).Adj v w ↔ G.Adj v w ∧ s(v, w) ∉ s#check deleteEdges_adj -- (G.deleteEdges s).Adj v w ↔ G.Adj v w ∧ s(v, w) ∉ s SimpleGraph.deleteEdges_edgeSet.{u_1} {V : Type u_1} (G G' : SimpleGraph V) : G.deleteEdges G'.edgeSet = G \ G'#check deleteEdges_edgeSet -- G.deleteEdges H.edgeSet = G \ H

2.6.1. Top and Bottom🔗

The complete graph ⊤ has all possible edges (every pair of distinct vertices is adjacent), while the empty graph ⊥ has no edges. These are the greatest and least elements of the subgraph order. Although completeGraph V and emptyGraph V are abbreviations for ⊤ and ⊥, we generally use top and bot in naming results about these graphs.

SimpleGraph.top_adj.{u} {V : Type u} (v w : V) : ⊤.Adj v w ↔ v ≠ w#check top_adj -- (⊤ : SimpleGraph V).Adj v w ↔ v ≠ w SimpleGraph.bot_adj.{u} {V : Type u} (v w : V) : ⊥.Adj v w ↔ False#check bot_adj -- (⊥ : SimpleGraph V).Adj v w ↔ False

Every graph is a subgraph of the complete graph.

example : G ≤ ⊤ := le_top

The empty graph is a subgraph of every graph.

example : ⊥ ≤ G := bot_le

If G is a proper subgraph of H then G is a proper subgraph of the complete graph.

example {G H : SimpleGraph V} (h : G < H) : G < ⊤ := lt_top_of_lt h end order end basics

Notice that the last few proofs all made use of results about orders rather than anything specific to graphs. They all follow easily from Mathlib's instance of CompleteAtomicBooleanAlgebra (SimpleGraph V), which we displayed with #synth at the start of this section.

2.7. Constructing a SimpleGraph🔗

The simplest way to build a SimpleGraph is with its default constructor: SimpleGraph.mk, supplying an adjacency relation together with proofs of symmetry and irreflexivity. In many cases (such as below) the tactic aesop_graph can discharge one or both proofs so they can be omitted. In this section we will look at three different ways of constructing the same graph: the path graph on ℕ.

The path graph on ℕ defined using the default constructor, with x and y adjacent iff x + 1 = y or y + 1 = x.

@[simps] abbrev pathNat : SimpleGraph ℕ where Adj x y := x + 1 = y ∨ y + 1 = x

The @[simps] attribute automatically generates the simp lemma pathNat_adj. An attribute, written @[…] before a declaration, tells Lean to do something extra with the declaration once it is defined: @[simp] registers a lemma for use by simp, and @[simps] generates simp lemmas from a definition. (If you want to see which lemmas are generated by a @[simps] attribute you can change it to @[simps?] and the InfoView will tell you.)

SimpleGraph.pathNat_adj (x y : ℕ) : pathNat.Adj x y = (x + 1 = y ∨ y + 1 = x)#check pathNat_adj -- pathNat.Adj x y = (x + 1 = y ∨ y + 1 = x)

Another way to construct the same graph is to use the SimpleGraph.fromRel constructor which symmetrizes any given relation and removes loops. The expression (· + 1 = ·) below is shorthand for the relation fun x y => x + 1 = y.

def SimpleGraph.fromRel {V : Type u} (r : V → V → Prop) : SimpleGraph V where Adj a b := a ≠ b ∧ (r a b ∨ r b a)#source SimpleGraph.fromRel

The path graph on ℕ defined using SimpleGraph.fromRel.

@[simps!] def pathNatFromRel : SimpleGraph ℕ := SimpleGraph.fromRel (· + 1 = ·)

This time we used @[simps!] rather than @[simps]. Plain @[simps] reads its lemmas straight off a definition written as a structure, as pathNat was (using where), since the value of each field is written out explicitly. The body of pathNatFromRel is instead an application of fromRel, so to find Adj it must first unfold fromRel and then tidy up the result with simp. The ! asks for both. (If we wrote @[simps] here, a linter warning would suggest @[simps!].)

SimpleGraph.pathNatFromRel_adj (a b : ℕ) : pathNatFromRel.Adj a b = (¬a = b ∧ (a + 1 = b ∨ b + 1 = a))#check pathNatFromRel_adj -- pathNatFromRel.Adj a b = -- (¬a = b ∧ (a + 1 = b ∨ b + 1 = a))

Also notice that pathNatFromRel is a def, whereas pathNat (and pathNatFromEdgeSet below) are abbrevs. The difference is that an abbrev is a definition that Lean unfolds automatically when it needs to. This is deliberate: we will see in Decidability, Finiteness and Degrees how this choice affects Lean's ability to compute with these graphs.

The two graphs pathNat and pathNatFromRel are equal, but not definitionally equal: rfl does not prove the equality. We explain this important distinction in Definitional and Propositional Equalities below.

In order to prove this we need to show that they have the same adjacency relation (i.e. the same edges). We don't need to check that they have the same vertex sets since this is done automatically by the type system: both pathNat and pathNatFromRel are SimpleGraph ℕ.

Lean's type checker ensures that we can't even state a theorem saying that two graphs with different vertex sets are equal. For example if G : SimpleGraph V then the expression G = pathNat is not well-typed since pathNat has vertex type ℕ and G has vertex type V.

/- error: Type mismatch pathNat has type SimpleGraph.{0} ℕ -/ example {V : Type*} (G : SimpleGraph V) : G = Type mismatch pathNat has type SimpleGraph.{0} ℕ of sort `Type` but is expected to have type SimpleGraph.{u_1} V of sort `Type u_1`pathNat := V:Type u_1G:SimpleGraph V⊢ sorry All goals completed! 🐙

Any two graphs on the same vertex type with the same edges are equal by extensionality, and we can use the ext tactic to prove that pathNat and pathNatFromRel are equal. The definition of SimpleGraph is tagged with the @[ext] attribute which gives us the following ext lemmas for free.

SimpleGraph.ext.{u} {V : Type u} {x y : SimpleGraph V} (Adj : x.Adj = y.Adj) : x = y#check SimpleGraph.ext SimpleGraph.ext_iff.{u} {V : Type u} {x y : SimpleGraph V} : x = y ↔ x.Adj = y.Adj#check SimpleGraph.ext_iff

The ext tactic reduces the goal to showing that for all a and b, pathNat.Adj a b ↔ pathNatFromRel.Adj a b. After rewriting with the two adjacency lemmas, what remains is a statement of logic and arithmetic about natural numbers, which grind proves. grind is an automated tactic that combines case splitting, congruence closure and linear arithmetic; we use it throughout this guide to finish off goals of this kind, and say more about it in Grind.

example : pathNat = pathNatFromRel := ⊢ pathNat = pathNatFromRel a:ℕb:ℕ⊢ pathNat.Adj a b ↔ pathNatFromRel.Adj a b -- now rewrite using the definition of adjacency in both graphs a:ℕb:ℕ⊢ a + 1 = b ∨ b + 1 = a ↔ ¬a = b ∧ (a + 1 = b ∨ b + 1 = a) -- the goal is now to show that the two relations are equivalent -- ⊢ a + 1 = b ∨ b + 1 = a ↔ ¬a = b ∧ (a + 1 = b ∨ b + 1 = a) All goals completed! 🐙

A third way to construct a SimpleGraph is from a set of edges s : Set (Sym2 V). (Recall that edges are unordered pairs of vertices, which have type Sym2 V in Lean.)

def fromEdgeSet : SimpleGraph V where Adj := Sym2.ToRel s ⊓ Ne symm.symm u v h := ⟨Sym2.toRel_symm s |>.symm u v h.left, h.right.symm⟩#source SimpleGraph.fromEdgeSet

The path graph on ℕ defined using SimpleGraph.fromEdgeSet.

@[simps!] abbrev pathNatFromEdgeSet : SimpleGraph ℕ := SimpleGraph.fromEdgeSet {e | ∃ n, e = s(n, n + 1)}

Again we can show that pathNatFromEdgeSet is equal to pathNat using ext (hence all three definitions agree).

lemma pathNat_eq_pathNatFromEdgeSet : pathNat = pathNatFromEdgeSet := ⊢ pathNat = pathNatFromEdgeSet a:ℕb:ℕ⊢ pathNat.Adj a b ↔ pathNatFromEdgeSet.Adj a b a:ℕb:ℕ⊢ a + 1 = b ∨ b + 1 = a ↔ (∃ n, a = n ∧ b = n + 1 ∨ a = n + 1 ∧ b = n) ∧ ¬a = b All goals completed! 🐙

We can also state this equality in terms of adjacency, which is usually more convenient.

lemma pathNat_adj_iff_pathNatFromEdgeSet {x y : ℕ} : pathNat.Adj x y ↔ pathNatFromEdgeSet.Adj x y := x:ℕy:ℕ⊢ pathNat.Adj x y ↔ pathNatFromEdgeSet.Adj x y All goals completed! 🐙

2.7.1. Definitional and Propositional Equalities🔗

All three of our path graphs are equal, but Lean distinguishes two kinds of equality. An equality a = b is definitional if both sides unfold to the same term, so that rfl proves it; we then say that a and b are definitionally equal, or defeq for short. Otherwise the equality is merely propositional: it may still be true, but it needs a genuine proof. (Every definitional equality is also propositional, with proof rfl.) The equality pathNat = pathNatFromRel is propositional but not definitional: we proved it with ext and a short argument about natural numbers, while rfl fails.

/- error: Tactic rfl failed: The left-hand side pathNat is not definitionally equal to the right-hand side pathNatFromRel -/ example : pathNat = pathNatFromRel := ⊢ pathNat = pathNatFromRel Tactic `rfl` failed: The left-hand side pathNat is not definitionally equal to the right-hand side pathNatFromRel ⊢ pathNat = pathNatFromRel⊢ pathNat = pathNatFromRel

Here unfolding means more than replacing names by their definitions: Lean also computes (or reduces), running any recursion or pattern match whose argument it can see is a constructor. For example + on ℕ is defined by recursion on its second argument, so n + 0 reduces to n even for a variable n, and rfl proves n + 0 = n. But in 0 + n the recursion is on the variable n, which is neither 0 nor a successor, so the computation is stuck: 0 + n = n is true, but only propositionally, and its proof needs induction on n.

example (n : ℕ) : n + 0 = n := n:ℕ⊢ n + 0 = n All goals completed! 🐙 /- error: Tactic rfl failed: The left-hand side 0 + n is not definitionally equal to the right-hand side n -/ example (n : ℕ) : 0 + n = n := n:ℕ⊢ 0 + n = n Tactic `rfl` failed: The left-hand side 0 + n is not definitionally equal to the right-hand side n n:ℕ⊢ 0 + n = nn:ℕ⊢ 0 + n = n

The distinction matters more in Lean than on paper. Lean's type checker, and its matching of terms when we apply a lemma, only see definitional equalities, so two things that are merely propositionally equal cannot be used interchangeably without an explicit step.

Definitionally equal statements, on the other hand, are interchangeable, and the change tactic lets us restate one as another: change t replaces the goal by t, provided the two are definitionally equal (and change t at h does the same for a hypothesis h). One use is to unfold a definition that automation cannot see through. Below, grind fails on the goal pathNatFromRel.Adj x (x + 1), but once change has unfolded pathNatFromRel and fromRel the goal is about natural numbers, and grind proves it. By contrast, change pathNat.Adj x (x + 1) would fail, since pathNat and pathNatFromRel are not definitionally equal.

example (x : ℕ) : pathNatFromRel.Adj x (x + 1) := x:ℕ⊢ pathNatFromRel.Adj x (x + 1) x:ℕ⊢ x ≠ x + 1 ∧ (x + 1 = x + 1 ∨ x + 1 + 1 = x) All goals completed! 🐙

Relying on how a definition happens to unfold is sometimes called defeq abuse. The proof above depends on the implementation of Mathlib's fromRel and might break if that changed, whereas rw [pathNatFromRel_adj] (or just simp) relies only on a stated lemma. So when a definition comes with lemmas describing it, prefer them, and keep change for goals where no such lemma is available.

2.7.2. The Simplifier🔗

The simp tactic, Lean's simplifier, will be one of our most frequently used tactics, so it is worth knowing how it works. It rewrites the goal using the lemmas in the simp set, which consists of all the lemmas tagged @[simp] (including those generated by @[simps]) in Mathlib and in the files we import. Each of these lemmas is an equation or an ↔, which simp uses to rewrite from left to right. It simplifies the parts of a term before the term itself, and keeps going until no lemma applies. If the goal has become True (for example an equation whose two sides are the same) then simp closes it. The most common variants are:

  • simp at h simplifies the hypothesis h instead of the goal;

  • simp [foo, h] also rewrites with the lemma foo and the hypothesis h, while simp [-foo] stops it from using the simp lemma foo;

  • simp_all simplifies the goal and all the hypotheses, using each hypothesis to simplify the others and the goal, and is applied until nothing changes;

  • simp only [foo, h] rewrites with just the listed lemmas and hypotheses.

simp? works exactly like simp, but also suggests a simp only call listing the lemmas that were actually used (clicking on the suggestion in the InfoView replaces simp? by it). Running it on the adjacency relations of our three path graphs gives three different answers.

example (a b : ℕ) : pathNatFromRel.Adj a b ↔ a ≠ b ∧ (a + 1 = b ∨ b + 1 = a) := a:ℕb:ℕ⊢ pathNatFromRel.Adj a b ↔ a ≠ b ∧ (a + 1 = b ∨ b + 1 = a) Try this: [apply] simp only [pathNatFromRel_adj, ne_eq]All goals completed! 🐙 -- Try this: simp only [pathNatFromRel_adj, ne_eq] example (a b : ℕ) : pathNat.Adj a b ↔ a + 1 = b ∨ b + 1 = a := a:ℕb:ℕ⊢ pathNat.Adj a b ↔ a + 1 = b ∨ b + 1 = a Try this: [apply] simp onlyAll goals completed! 🐙 -- Try this: simp only example (a b : ℕ) : pathNatFromEdgeSet.Adj a b ↔ (∃ n, a = n ∧ b = n + 1 ∨ a = n + 1 ∧ b = n) ∧ a ≠ b := a:ℕb:ℕ⊢ pathNatFromEdgeSet.Adj a b ↔ (∃ n, a = n ∧ b = n + 1 ∨ a = n + 1 ∧ b = n) ∧ a ≠ b Try this: [apply] simp only [fromEdgeSet_adj, Set.mem_ofPred_eq, Sym2.eq, Sym2.rel_iff', Prod.mk.injEq, Prod.swap_prod_mk, ne_eq]All goals completed! 🐙 -- Try this: simp only [fromEdgeSet_adj, Set.mem_ofPred_eq, Sym2.eq, ...]

Two things determine what simp does here: whether it can see inside the definition, and what it finds there. simp does not unfold a def (unless we ask it to, with simp [pathNatFromRel]), so all it can do with pathNatFromRel.Adj a b is rewrite it using a lemma. It uses pathNatFromRel_adj, which @[simps!] generated for exactly this purpose. An abbrev, on the other hand, is unfolded by simp, and what happens next depends on its body. The body of pathNat is a structure with its Adj field written out, so simp reads pathNat.Adj a b straight off it, without using any lemma at all. The body of pathNatFromEdgeSet is fromEdgeSet s for a set of edges s, so simp sees (fromEdgeSet s).Adj a b and rewrites it with Mathlib's lemma fromEdgeSet_adj (and then tidies up the result).

So simp never uses pathNat_adj or pathNatFromEdgeSet_adj. They are still useful as named lemmas, for example with rw in the proofs above: pathNatFromEdgeSet_adj states adjacency in a tidied-up form, whereas rewriting with fromEdgeSet_adj would leave a goal about Sym2.

In fact Mathlib would not accept pathNatFromEdgeSet_adj as a simp lemma. If another simp lemma also applies to the left-hand side of a simp lemma, then simp may use that one instead, and the lemma never gets used. So the left-hand side of a simp lemma should be in simp normal form: no other simp lemma should apply to it. The left-hand side pathNatFromEdgeSet.Adj a b fails this test, since the simp lemma fromEdgeSet_adj applies to it. Mathlib checks every simp lemma for this with its simpNF linter, which you can run on your own file with #lint only simpNF. We will meet simp normal forms again in Copy.

simp? has a second use. The simp set grows as Mathlib does, so a plain simp may do something different in a future version of Mathlib. That's fine if simp closes the goal, but if later steps depend on exactly what simp produced then the proof may break. So the convention in Mathlib is that a non-terminal simp, one that does not close the goal, should be a simp only. Mathlib's flexible linter, which is enabled for this guide, warns about a non-terminal simp (its warning calls simp a flexible tactic) and suggests using simp?. For example, if a + 1 and b + 1 are adjacent in pathNat then so are a and b, but the following proof of this triggers the warning.

example (a b : ℕ) (h : pathNat.Adj (a + 1) (b + 1)) : pathNat.Adj a b := a:ℕb:ℕh:pathNat.Adj (a + 1) (b + 1)⊢ pathNat.Adj a b `simp at h` is a flexible tactic modifying `h`. Try `simp?` and use the suggested `simp only [...]`. Alternatively, use `suffices` to explicitly state the simplified form. Note: This linter can be disabled with `set_option linter.flexible false`a:ℕb:ℕh:a + 1 = b ∨ b + 1 = a⊢ pathNat.Adj a b `exact h` uses `h`, which was modified by the flexible tactic `simp` on line 776!All goals completed! 🐙

Following its advice and running simp? leads to a proof that does not depend on the rest of the simp set.

example (a b : ℕ) (h : pathNat.Adj (a + 1) (b + 1)) : pathNat.Adj a b := a:ℕb:ℕh:pathNat.Adj (a + 1) (b + 1)⊢ pathNat.Adj a b a:ℕb:ℕh:a + 1 = b ∨ b + 1 = a⊢ pathNat.Adj a b All goals completed! 🐙

Often a neater fix is to let simp finish the proof. simpa using e simplifies both the goal and the type of e, then closes the goal with e (and simpa [foo] using e also rewrites with the lemma foo). Without the simplification exact h would fail, since h and the goal only agree once both have been simplified.

example (a b : ℕ) (h : pathNat.Adj (a + 1) (b + 1)) : pathNat.Adj a b := a:ℕb:ℕh:pathNat.Adj (a + 1) (b + 1)⊢ pathNat.Adj a b All goals completed! 🐙

2.7.3. Grind🔗

grind is the other automated tactic we use throughout this guide, and it works quite differently from simp. Rather than rewriting the goal, it assumes that the goal is false and looks for a contradiction. Along the way it collects facts, keeps track of which terms are equal, splits into cases, applies lemmas whenever it meets terms that match them, and uses built-in procedures for linear arithmetic over ℕ and ℤ and for algebra in commutative rings. It only ever finishes a goal: if it cannot, it fails and lists the facts it had collected, which often shows what it was missing.

grind does not use the simp set. Unlike simp, it always uses all the hypotheses in the local context (so passing one, as in grind [h], is an error). Apart from these and its built-in reasoning, it only uses the lemmas tagged with a grind attribute and those we pass to it, as in grind [foo, bar]. Very few of Mathlib's lemmas about graphs are tagged for grind, which is why our grind calls often list lemmas.

Like simp, grind unfolds an abbrev but not a def.

example (x : ℕ) : pathNat.Adj x (x + 1) := x:ℕ⊢ pathNat.Adj x (x + 1) All goals completed! 🐙 example (x : ℕ) : pathNatFromRel.Adj x (x + 1) := x:ℕ⊢ pathNatFromRel.Adj x (x + 1) All goals completed! 🐙 example (x : ℕ) : pathNatFromEdgeSet.Adj x (x + 1) := x:ℕ⊢ pathNatFromEdgeSet.Adj x (x + 1) All goals completed! 🐙

Plain grind fails on the last two goals: it cannot see inside the def pathNatFromRel. It does unfold the abbrev pathNatFromEdgeSet, but Mathlib's fromEdgeSet_adj is not a grind lemma, so it is left with a set of edges in Sym2 ℕ that it cannot work with. For the last goal grind [fromEdgeSet_adj] would also work, but the tidied-up statement of pathNatFromEdgeSet_adj (the lemma that simp never uses) is more useful in general. With it, grind proves that pathNat and pathNatFromEdgeSet are equal without rewriting first, whereas grind [fromEdgeSet_adj] fails here.

example : pathNat = pathNatFromEdgeSet := ⊢ pathNat = pathNatFromEdgeSet a:ℕb:ℕ⊢ pathNat.Adj a b ↔ pathNatFromEdgeSet.Adj a b All goals completed! 🐙

Like simp?, grind? suggests a call grind only [...] that uses just the lemmas that were needed (it may also offer other forms of the call).

example (x : ℕ) : pathNatFromRel.Adj x (x + 1) := x:ℕ⊢ pathNatFromRel.Adj x (x + 1) Try these: [apply] grind only [pathNatFromRel_adj] [apply] grind => instantiate only [pathNatFromRel_adj]All goals completed! 🐙 -- Try these: grind only [pathNatFromRel_adj], ...

Instead of passing a lemma to each grind call, we can tag it with a grind attribute, so that every later grind call can use it. Most such tags in Mathlib are @[grind =], on equations or ↔s characterizing a definition (like pathNatFromRel_adj): grind then uses the lemma whenever it meets a term matching its left-hand side. (Similarly @[grind →] uses an implication whenever it meets terms matching its hypotheses.) Here we add the attribute for a single example only, with attribute [local grind =] … in.

attribute [local grind =] pathNatFromRel_adj in example (x : ℕ) : pathNatFromRel.Adj x (x + 1) := x:ℕ⊢ pathNatFromRel.Adj x (x + 1) All goals completed! 🐙

Tags should be added sparingly, since they affect every later grind call, and a lemma that matches too many terms can make grind slow. The command #grind_lint inspect foo warns if the lemma foo leads grind into long chains of lemma applications. In this guide we do not tag any lemmas for grind. Instead each call lists the lemmas it needs, which also shows the reader which facts the proof uses.

Finally, grind is not designed for problems that need a huge number of case splits, such as checking by brute force that a particular graph has no 3-colouring. For finite checks like this we use decide, introduced in Decidability, Finiteness and Degrees.

2.8. Computations🔗

As well as reasoning about graphs in Lean we can also do computations with them. For example we can check that 0 and 3 are adjacent in the complete graph on Fin 5 (the type consisting of {0, 1, 2, 3, 4}).

true#eval (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin 5)).Adj 0 3 -- true

We can count edges in finite graphs. For example the completeGraph on Fin 6 has 15 edges.

15#eval (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin 6)).edgeFinset.card -- 15

Even when our goal is to prove theorems, computations such as these can be very useful. Firstly, they allow us to perform quick sanity checks of our definitions and secondly they can be used inside proofs with the decide tactic.

example : (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin 6)).Adj 2 3 := ⊢ ⊤.Adj 2 3 All goals completed! 🐙

Both #eval and decide rely on adjacency being decidable: Lean needs a concrete method for deciding whether or not any given pair of vertices are adjacent. We will return to this, and to computations with graphs more generally, in Decidability, Finiteness and Degrees.

  1. Show that the edge set of pathNat is {e | ∃ n, e = s(n, n + 1)}. Hint: use induction e using Sym2.ind.

declaration uses `sorry`example (G H : SimpleGraph V) : G ≤ H ↔ Hᶜ ≤ Gᶜ := V:Type u_1G:SimpleGraph VH:SimpleGraph V⊢ G ≤ H ↔ Hᶜ ≤ Gᶜ All goals completed! 🐙

declaration uses `sorry`example : (⊤ : SimpleGraph V)ᶜ = ⊥ := V:Type u_1⊢ ⊤ᶜ = ⊥ All goals completed! 🐙

In the next few exercises we follow a convention that we will use throughout this guide. We use a prime, as in shiftedPathNat', to denote a version of a definition or result that contains a sorry. This is so that we can use the same names (without a prime) in the solutions below, thus ensuring that when we refer to them in later chapters they resolve to the correct definition.

  1. For i : ℕ, define the graph shiftedPathNat' i to be a SimpleGraph ℕ with edges from n to n + 1 iff i ≤ n. (If aesop_graph can prove the symm and loopless fields for your definition then you can simply delete those two lines.)

Solutions

  1. Show that the edge set of pathNat is {e | ∃ n, e = s(n, n + 1)}. Hint: use induction e using Sym2.ind.

example : pathNat.edgeSet = {e | ∃ n, e = s(n, n + 1)} := ⊢ pathNat.edgeSet = {e | ∃ n, e = s(n, n + 1)} e:Sym2 ℕ⊢ e ∈ pathNat.edgeSet ↔ e ∈ {e | ∃ n, e = s(n, n + 1)} induction e using Sym2.ind with x:ℕy:ℕ⊢ s(x, y) ∈ pathNat.edgeSet ↔ s(x, y) ∈ {e | ∃ n, e = s(n, n + 1)} x:ℕy:ℕ⊢ x + 1 = y ∨ y + 1 = x ↔ ∃ n, x = n ∧ y = n + 1 ∨ x = n + 1 ∧ y = n; All goals completed! 🐙

  1. For i : ℕ, define the graph shiftedPathNat i to be a SimpleGraph ℕ with edges from n to n + 1 iff i ≤ n. (If aesop_graph can prove the symm and loopless fields for your definition then you can simply delete those two lines.)

Notice we don't need to give proofs of symm and loopless, since aesop_graph can prove these.

The graph on ℕ with an edge from n to n + 1 whenever i ≤ n.

@[simps] def shiftedPathNat (i : ℕ) : SimpleGraph ℕ where Adj n m := n + 1 = m ∧ i ≤ n ∨ m + 1 = n ∧ i ≤ m

The graph on ℕ with an edge from n to n + 1 whenever n < i.

@[simps] def shortPathNat (i : ℕ) : SimpleGraph ℕ where Adj n m := n + 1 = m ∧ n < i ∨ m + 1 = n ∧ m < i
